cards.title: A careful way to test
cards.body: Ping the local interface, then the default gateway, then a host on another local subnet, then a remote address, then a name (which also tests DNS). That order — sometimes called a divide-and-conquer or bottom-up habit — stops you from blaming DNS when the cable is unplugged. Traceroute comes in once you know the far end is the problem, not the local NIC.

cards.title: What a failed ping does not prove
cards.body: No reply can mean the host is down, an address is wrong, a firewall is dropping ICMP, or a return path is missing. It does not, on its own, prove that 'the internet is down'. Combine ping with interface status, ARP or ND tables, and the routing table before you change a lot of configuration.

quiz.q: A successful ping shows that:
options: Echo Request and Echo Reply can travel between the two addresses (so a basic IP path exists)
Every TCP and UDP port on the target is open
quiz.why: Ping tests ICMP echo, not web ports or DNS. A reply is strong evidence of a working IP path for that traffic; a failure is more ambiguous.

quiz.q: On IPv4, Echo Request and Echo Reply are ICMP types:
quiz.why: Type 8 is request, type 0 is reply. Types 128 and 129 are the ICMPv6 echo pair. 3 is destination unreachable; 11 is time exceeded.

quiz.q: Traceroute discovers hops by:
options: Sending packets with increasing TTL (or Hop Limit) and reading ICMP Time Exceeded replies
Asking a DNS server for a list of routers
Reading the switch MAC table only
Opening TCP port 80 on every router
quiz.why: Each router along the path is forced to expire a packet and report itself. That is the whole mechanism.

quiz.q: Windows `tracert` typically probes with:
quiz.why: Classic Windows tracert uses ICMP. Many Unix and Cisco traceroute implementations send UDP probes to a high port instead. The replies you care about are still ICMP.

quiz.q: If a router decrements TTL to zero, it should:
options: Drop the packet and usually send an ICMP Time Exceeded message to the sender
quiz.why: That is how loops are contained, and how traceroute gets its per-hop replies.

quiz.q: ICMPv6 Next Header (or protocol) number is:
quiz.why: 1 is ICMPv4, 6 is TCP, 17 is UDP, 58 is ICMPv6.

quiz.q: A Destination Unreachable message is useful because it can tell you:
options: That a network, host or port could not be reached, or that a packet was too large
The exact purchase date of the switch
That encryption is enabled on the link
quiz.why: The ICMP code adds a reason — net unreachable, host unreachable, port unreachable, packet too big, and others.

quiz.q: Blocking all ICMPv6 on an IPv6 LAN is a bad idea because:
options: Neighbour Discovery and other core IPv6 functions use ICMPv6, not just ping
IPv6 cannot run without IPv4 ICMP type 8
quiz.why: NS, NA, RS and RA are ICMPv6. Filter carefully if you must; do not treat ICMP as optional on IPv6 the way some people treat IPv4 ping.

quiz.q: A Cisco IOS ping that prints `.....` (five dots) means:
options: Each request timed out; no reply arrived in time
quiz.why: Exclamation marks are successes; dots are timeouts. You still have to find out why: wrong address, filtering, or a broken path.

quiz.q: A good first ping when a host 'cannot get to the internet' is:
options: Its default gateway (and then walk further out)
A random IPv6 multicast on another continent
The serial number of the office printer
quiz.why: If the gateway does not reply, fixing 'the internet' is the wrong job. Start close, then move out, then test names (DNS).

modules.title: Transport Layer
modules.blurb: TCP and UDP, port numbers, the three-way handshake, and when to use each protocol.

cards.title: The transport layer talks to processes, not just hosts
cards.body: IP gets a packet to the right **host**. The **transport layer** gets the data to the right **process** on that host. It does that with **port numbers**. Two main protocols do the work: **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) and **UDP** (User Datagram Protocol).

cards.title: TCP is reliable and connection-oriented
cards.body: TCP sets up a connection before it carries user data, numbers each **segment**, **acknowledges** what has arrived, **resends** what has not, and slows down when the receiver or the network is under pressure (**flow control** and congestion control). Use it when missing or reordered data would be a problem: web pages, email, file transfer, SSH.

cards.title: UDP is simple and connectionless
cards.body: UDP sends a **datagram** and does not set up a session, does not retransmit, and does not adjust a window. The header is only **8 bytes** (source port, destination port, length, checksum). That low overhead is why **DNS queries**, **DHCP**, **TFTP** and many voice or video streams use UDP. If something must be reliable, the application has to handle it.

cards.title: Port numbers
cards.body: A port is a 16-bit number (0–65535). The **destination port** says which service you want (443 for HTTPS, 53 for DNS). The **source port** is usually an **ephemeral** port chosen by the client so the reply can find the right conversation. Together, the two IPs, the two ports and the protocol (TCP or UDP) identify a conversation, sometimes called a socket pair.

cards.title: IANA port ranges
cards.body: IANA splits the space into **system (well-known) ports 0–1023**, **user (registered) ports 1024–49151**, and **dynamic/private ports 49152–65535**. Servers usually listen on a well-known or registered port. Clients usually pick a dynamic port. Some operating systems still use a wider ephemeral range; if a question asks for the IANA ranges, use the three bands above.

cards.title: The TCP three-way handshake
cards.body: To start a connection: the client sends a segment with **SYN**, the server replies with **SYN-ACK**, and the client sends **ACK**. Only after that do they send the stream of data. The flags are bits in the TCP header; you will also meet **FIN** (I am finished sending), **RST** (abort), **PSH** and **URG**.
cards.analogy: You ring a doorbell (SYN), the host opens the door and says hello (SYN-ACK), and you say hello back (ACK) before you start the actual conversation.

cards.title: Ending a TCP connection
cards.body: A polite close uses **FIN** and **ACK** in each direction (four segments in the full case), because each side has its own stream to close. A **RST** aborts at once, which is what you often see when a port is closed or a firewall rejects the session.

cards.title: Sequence numbers, ACKs and the window
cards.body: Each TCP byte has a **sequence number**. An **acknowledgement** tells the sender the next byte the receiver expects. The **window** says how many bytes may be in flight before the sender has to wait. If the window shrinks to zero, the sender pauses — that is **flow control**. Retransmissions use timers and missing ACKs to spot lost data.

cards.title: When a question asks 'TCP or UDP?'
cards.body: Ask: does this application already need speed more than guaranteed delivery, or would a lost bit ruin the file? Web (HTTP/HTTPS), email (SMTP, IMAP, POP3), FTP and SSH are TCP. DNS queries are usually UDP (and fall back to TCP for large answers or zone transfers). DHCP and TFTP are UDP. Voice is often UDP with the application hiding a lost packet.

cards.title: A UDP 'session' is just the ports
cards.body: UDP has no handshake, so a server process simply listens on a port and a client sends a datagram to it. The server replies to the source IP and source port it saw. If a reply is lost, the client application may retry — DNS resolvers do this all the time — but UDP itself will not.

quiz.q: The transport layer uses port numbers to:
options: Deliver data to the correct process on a host
quiz.why: Ports are the Layer 4 address. IP gets you to the host; the port gets you to the application.

quiz.q: Which statement about TCP is right?
options: It is connection-oriented and can retransmit lost data
It has an 8-byte header and never retransmits
It replaces the need for IP addresses
quiz.why: TCP sets up a connection, numbers data, acknowledges it and resends on loss. UDP is the lightweight, no-retransmission protocol.

quiz.q: A UDP header is:
options: 8 bytes: source port, destination port, length and checksum
20 bytes or more, like a typical TCP header
40 bytes, like the IPv6 base header
quiz.why: Those four fields are the entire UDP header. That simplicity is the point.

quiz.q: The IANA well-known (system) port range is:
quiz.why: 0–1023 system, 1024–49151 registered, 49152–65535 dynamic. Memorise all three; questions like to swap them.

quiz.q: The three-way handshake, in order, is:
options: ACK, then SYN, then data only
UDP query, then ARP, then SYN
quiz.why: Client SYN, server SYN-ACK, client ACK. Data follows once the connection is open.

quiz.q: Flow control in TCP is mainly about:
options: The receiver advertising a window so the sender does not overwhelm it
Selecting a fibre or copper path
quiz.why: The window size tells the sender how much unacknowledged data is allowed. A window of zero means 'stop for now'.

quiz.q: DNS queries on the public internet are typically sent with:
options: UDP port 53 (using TCP 53 when the answer is large or for zone transfers)
quiz.why: Port 53 is DNS. UDP is the usual query transport; TCP is used as a fallback and for zone transfers. 67 is DHCP server, 22 is SSH, 80 is HTTP.

quiz.q: Which application is the best fit for UDP among these options?
options: A live voice stream that can tolerate a lost packet better than a delay
A bank file transfer that must not be missing a single byte
Downloading a software update with HTTPS
quiz.why: A late voice packet is often useless, so a simple, low-delay transport is attractive. Files, SSH and HTTPS need reliability and so use TCP.

quiz.q: A polite TCP close uses which flag to mean 'I have no more data to send'?
quiz.why: FIN finishes a stream. SYN starts a connection. RST aborts. PSH is a hint to pass data up promptly.

quiz.q: The source port on a typical client request is:
options: An ephemeral (dynamic) port chosen by the client for this conversation
The same as the well-known destination port
quiz.why: The destination port selects the service (for example 443). The source port lets the client tell several conversations apart when the replies come back.

modules.title: Application Layer
modules.blurb: The everyday services: web, email, DNS, DHCP and file transfer, and the ports they use.

cards.title: Where the application layer sits
cards.body: In the TCP/IP model, the **application layer** is everything the user or a program sees: the protocol that carries a web page, an email, a name lookup or a file. In OSI terms this also covers **presentation** (format, encryption, compression) and **session** (starting and ending a dialogue). You configure and troubleshoot these services by name and by port, not by 'Layer 6'.

cards.title: Client–server and peer-to-peer
cards.body: In a **client–server** model, a dedicated server listens for requests (a web server, a DNS server). In a **peer-to-peer** model, hosts act as both client and server for each other (many file-sharing and some collaboration tools). Home networks often mix both: your laptop is a client of a web server, and also a peer if you share a folder.

cards.title: The web: HTTP and HTTPS
cards.body: **HTTP** usually uses **TCP port 80** and sends requests (GET, POST and others) for resources. **HTTPS** is HTTP inside a TLS-protected session, usually on **TCP port 443**. A URL such as `https://learn.solent.ac.uk` already names the protocol, the host to resolve, and (implicitly) the port.

cards.title: Email is several protocols, not one
cards.body: **SMTP** (TCP **25** between servers; often **587** for a client submitting mail) sends a message on its way. To read mail, a client typically uses **IMAP** (TCP **143**, or **993** with TLS) which keeps mail on the server, or **POP3** (TCP **110**, or **995** with TLS) which often downloads and may remove it. Mixing these up is a common exam trap.

cards.title: DNS turns names into addresses
cards.body: People use names; packets use addresses. A **resolver** on your host asks a DNS server, usually on **port 53**. An **A** record maps a name to an IPv4 address; an **AAAA** record maps it to IPv6. If DNS is broken, 'the internet is down' often still pings by address — which is a clue to test with `nslookup` or `dig`, not only with a browser.

cards.title: DHCP hands out IPv4 settings automatically
cards.body: **DHCP** uses a four-step process often remembered as **DORA**: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. Messages use **UDP port 67** on the server and **UDP port 68** on the client. A successful lease gives the host an address, mask, default gateway and usually a DNS server, for a limited time (the lease).

cards.title: File transfer: FTP and TFTP
cards.body: **FTP** uses **TCP port 21** for control, and **TCP port 20** for the data connection in active mode (passive mode uses a different, negotiated data port). It can list directories and resume transfers, and it sends credentials in the clear unless wrapped in TLS. **TFTP** uses **UDP port 69**, is much simpler, and is often used to copy IOS images or configurations in a lab — with no login and no extra reliability of its own.

cards.title: A port table worth practising as flashcards
cards.body: 20/21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 67/68 DHCP, 69 TFTP, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 143 IMAP, 443 HTTPS. SNMP (161/162) and NTP (123) are also worth knowing. The Cards tab drills these until they are automatic.

cards.title: When a service 'does not work'
cards.body: Ask three questions. Is the name resolving (DNS)? Is the address reachable (ping or a hop-by-hop check)? Is the port actually open and permitted (a firewall or a service that is not running will fail here even if ping works)? That sequence stops you from reinstalling a browser when the problem is a typo in the DHCP DNS field.

quiz.q: HTTPS typically uses:
quiz.why: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, almost always on TCP 443. TCP 80 is plain HTTP. (HTTP/3 can use UDP 443, but the standard ITN answer for HTTPS is TCP 443.)

quiz.q: Which pair is right for DHCP?
options: UDP 67 on the server, UDP 68 on the client
quiz.why: BOOTP/DHCP reserved those two ports: 67 the server, 68 the client.

quiz.q: The four steps of a typical IPv4 DHCP handshake are:
quiz.why: DORA is the standard memory aid for DHCP. SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK is the TCP handshake, which is a different process.

quiz.q: An AAAA record in DNS maps a name to:
quiz.why: A is IPv4, AAAA is IPv6. That is the whole distinction.

quiz.q: Which protocol is primarily used to send email between servers?
quiz.why: SMTP is the sending and relaying protocol. IMAP and POP3 are how a client reads or collects mail.

quiz.q: IMAP is often preferred over POP3 in a student or work setting because:
options: It is designed to keep mail on the server and stay in sync from several devices
It uses UDP and is therefore faster in every case
It replaces the need for SMTP
quiz.why: IMAP works with a mailbox that stays on the server. POP3 traditionally downloads (and may delete) messages, which is awkward if you use a phone and a laptop.

quiz.q: TFTP, as used in many Cisco labs, runs on:
quiz.why: TFTP is the lightweight, UDP-based file transfer protocol on port 69. FTP control is TCP 21; SSH is TCP 22; DHCP server is UDP 67.

quiz.q: A browser cannot open a named website, but ping to the site's IP address works. The most likely first suspect is:
options: That IPv4 has been removed from the internet
A failed enable secret on your laptop
quiz.why: Ping by address already proved a path. Failure by name points at DNS (or a typo in the name).

quiz.q: FTP's well-known control port is:
options: TCP 21 (with TCP 20 used for data in active mode)
quiz.why: Control = 21, active-mode data = 20. Passive mode negotiates a different data port. TFTP is the one on UDP 69.

quiz.q: In the TCP/IP model, HTTP, DNS and SMTP sit at the:
quiz.why: Those are application protocols. The internet layer is IP. Network access is the link and the physical medium.

modules.title: Network Security Fundamentals
modules.blurb: Common threats, and the basic hardening steps you should apply to a switch or router.

cards.title: Why a lab device still needs hardening
cards.body: A switch or router is a powerful target: anyone who controls it can listen, redirect or cut off traffic. Even on a small network you should assume that default passwords, unused services and clear-text logins will be tried. Security is one of the four requirements of a reliable network, not an optional extra.

cards.title: A short map of threats
cards.body: **Malware** is software that does harm (viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware). **Social engineering** attacks the person, not the packet (phishing is the common example). **Denial of service (DoS)** tries to exhaust a link or a host so nobody else can use it. **Spoofing** means pretending to be another address or device (fake ARP, fake IP, fake emails). You do not need a long catalogue in ITN, but you should be able to recognise each of these words.

cards.title: Defence is layered
cards.body: No single control is enough. Combine **physical** security (who can touch the console), **device** hardening (passwords, SSH, unused ports), **network** controls (firewalls, private addressing, perhaps ACLs later in the CCNA path), and **user** habits (updates, scepticism about unexpected links). If one layer fails, the next should still help.

cards.title: Passwords, done properly
cards.body: Use **`enable secret`** rather than `enable password`. Use **`service password-encryption`** so casual readers of the config do not see line passwords in the clear — and remember that type 7 is weak. Prefer **SSH** to Telnet, and use a **local username** (`username ... secret ...` plus `login local` on the VTY lines) rather than a shared line password alone. Do not leave default credentials in place.

cards.title: SSH rather than Telnet
cards.body: Telnet (TCP 23) sends every keystroke, including passwords, in the clear. **SSH** (TCP 22) encrypts the session. A typical setup is: set a domain name, generate an RSA key pair, create a local user, and on the VTY lines use `transport input ssh` and `login local`. Then shut Telnet off. Console access still needs its own password, because a person with a cable can walk up to the device.

cards.title: Banners, unused ports, unused services
cards.body: A **banner motd** should warn that access is authorised only — it is a legal and practical notice, not a decoration. On a switch, **shutdown unused ports** and put them in an unused VLAN if you can. Turn off services you do not use. Every open door you forget is a door somebody else can try.

cards.title: Keep the software and the clock honest
cards.body: Running a current, supported **IOS** image with known fixes is part of hardening, not a luxury. A correct clock (and later, NTP) makes logs meaningful when you investigate an incident. Back up the configuration to a safe place so that a mistake or a failed upgrade is recoverable.

cards.title: What this module is not
cards.body: ITN does not expect you to configure a full firewall policy or an intrusion-prevention system. It does expect you to stop making the easy mistakes: empty passwords, Telnet, unused ports left up, a running-config that has never been saved or backed up, and a banner that claims 'welcome, please come in'. Get those right on every lab device, every time.

quiz.q: Which login method encrypts the session, including passwords, as you type?
options: A banner motd on its own
An unconfigured VTY line with no login
quiz.why: SSH (port 22) is encrypted. Telnet (port 23) is clear text and should not be used on a network you care about.

quiz.q: Why is `enable secret` preferred to `enable password`?
options: The secret is stored as a hash, not as recoverable plain text
The password command encrypts traffic on the wire
They are identical in every IOS release
quiz.why: A hashed secret is the right way to protect privileged EXEC. `enable password` is a legacy, weaker option.

quiz.q: Phishing is an example of:
options: Social engineering — attacking the person rather than a protocol bug
quiz.why: The message tries to trick a human into giving up a password or clicking something dangerous. The protocol may be working perfectly.

quiz.q: A denial-of-service attack aims to:
options: Exhaust a resource so legitimate users cannot get a service
quiz.why: DoS is about availability: fill a link, a CPU or a table until the service is unusable.

quiz.q: A sensible way to treat unused switch ports is to:
options: Shut them down (and, if you can, place them in an unused VLAN)
Leave them up so visitors can plug in without asking
Configure them with the default VLAN and a DHCP helper as a courtesy
Mirror every unused port to the internet
quiz.why: An unused open port is a convenient place for someone to attach an unauthorised device. Shutdown is the basic control.

quiz.q: The usual TCP port for SSH is:
quiz.why: 22 is SSH, 23 is Telnet, 80 is HTTP, 69 is TFTP.

quiz.q: `service password-encryption` should be understood as:
options: A weak, reversible disguise of some passwords in the configuration file
Strong hashing equal to a modern enable secret
Encryption of every packet on every interface
quiz.why: Type 7 is better than nothing on a casual glance at the screen, but it is not strong cryptography. Use secrets and SSH as well.

quiz.q: A banner motd is useful because it:
options: Displays a warning that only authorised users should access the device
Encrypts the enable secret a second time
Replaces the need for a console password
quiz.why: The banner is a notice (and often a legal warning). It does not authenticate anyone on its own.

quiz.q: Spoofing, in the sense used here, means:
options: Pretending to be another address or device, for example with a fake ARP reply
Compressing a packet to save bandwidth
Setting a hostname that matches a building name
quiz.why: A spoofed source (IP, MAC, email) is a lie about identity. ARP spoofing is a common LAN example.

quiz.q: To require SSH and a local user on the VTY lines, you would include:
options: login local and transport input ssh, plus a username secret and generated keys
no login, so anyone can attach
quiz.why: Keys, a local user, `login local`, and `transport input ssh` together make a basic encrypted remote login. Telnet-only is the opposite of the goal.

modules.title: Build a Small Network
modules.blurb: Putting the pieces together: devices, verification commands, and a calm troubleshooting order.

cards.title: The small network is the pattern for larger ones
cards.body: A typical small network still has **end devices**, one or more **switches**, a **router** (or a combined router and firewall), and maybe a wireless access point. Addressing, default gateways, basic security and verification do not change just because a later network has more floors. If you can design, build and fix this, you have the habit the rest of CCNA builds on.

cards.title: Plan before you plug in
cards.body: Write down the hostname, the LAN prefix, the gateway address, the management address of the switch, and which ports go where. Give each interface a **description**. Decide on SSH, secrets and a banner as part of the plan, not as an afterthought. Most lab failures are planning failures, not mysterious IOS bugs.

cards.title: Scale without starting again
cards.body: A network grows more cleanly if you have already thought about **hierarchical** design: an access layer where hosts plug in, and (as you grow) distribution and core layers that you will meet properly later in the CCNA path. Leaving spare ports, spare addresses and documented VLANs (when you start using them) is cheaper than a redesign.

cards.title: Verification is a short toolkit
cards.body: On a host: `ipconfig` / `ip addr`, `ping`, `tracert` / `traceroute`, `arp -a`, `nslookup`. On IOS: `show ip interface brief`, `show ipv6 interface brief`, `show ip route`, `show ip arp`, `show mac address-table`, `show running-config`, `show version`. You do not need every option of every command. You need to know which command answers which question.

cards.title: Ping and traceroute, used as a pair
cards.body: Ping answers 'can I get there and back, right now, for ICMP?' Traceroute answers 'which hop is the last good one, and where does it go quiet?' Read both: a ping failure at the gateway is a different job from a traceroute that dies three hops into a provider network.

cards.title: Three troubleshooting orders
cards.body: **Bottom-up** starts at the physical layer (cables, lights, interfaces) and climbs. **Top-down** starts at the application (the browser, the name, the port) and works down. **Divide and conquer** starts in the middle, often at the network layer (can I ping the gateway? can I ping by address?). There is no single correct religion; pick one and be consistent, so you do not change three things at once.

cards.title: A practical sequence for 'it does not connect'
cards.body: Is the interface up/up? Right cable, right port, right speed and duplex? Does the host have a sensible address, mask and gateway (`ipconfig`)? Can it ping the gateway? Is the ARP or ND entry there? Can it ping a remote address? Can it resolve a name? Only then blame the application. If you change something, change one thing, then test again.

cards.title: Show commands that describe the device itself
cards.body: `show version` tells you the software and the uptime. `show running-config` is the live truth of your settings. `show startup-config` is what will load after a reload — compare the two if a change 'vanished'. On a host, `hostname` / the computer name, and the output of `ipconfig /all`, play a similar role.

cards.title: How this app fits next to NetAcad
cards.body: The explainers and quizzes here are for understanding and recall. Packet Tracer and the NetAcad labs are where you build the muscle memory on real (or simulated) devices. When a quiz answer is solid but a lab still fails, it is almost always a typo, an unsaved config, or a step skipped in verification — not a sign that you should start the module again from scratch.

quiz.q: A small office network will almost always include at least:
options: End devices, a switch, and a router (or a device that can route) toward other networks
A unique fibre run from every PC to the internet, with no LAN
A separate router for each printer, and nothing else
quiz.why: Hosts, a LAN switch, and a router (which may be combined with a firewall or wireless AP) is the basic shape.

quiz.q: Which IOS command is the fastest way to see interface addresses and up/down state?
quiz.why: `show ip interface brief` is the standard first glance after cabling and addressing.

quiz.q: A host can ping a dotted-decimal address but cannot open a website by name. You should next check:
options: DNS (for example with nslookup), and the DNS server setting from DHCP
Whether the patch cable exists at all
The colour of the device hostname
The enable secret on a core switch in another country
quiz.why: Ping by address already showed a path. A name failure is DNS until proven otherwise.

quiz.q: Bottom-up troubleshooting starts with:
options: The physical layer: cables, lights and interface status
The application, for example a web URL
A full factory reset of every device
quiz.why: Bottom-up climbs the stack from Layer 1. Top-down starts at the application. Both are valid if you stick to them.

quiz.q: Divide and conquer, as a troubleshooting habit, often means:
options: Testing a middle layer first (for example pinging a gateway) to see which half of the path is broken
Changing every setting on every device before testing
Only ever using traceroute, never ping
quiz.why: A single mid-stack test can tell you whether to look downward (local link, addressing) or upward (application, DNS, ports).

quiz.q: If running-config looks right but the same setting is gone after a reload, the usual cause is:
options: The running configuration was never copied to the startup configuration
IPv6 has been banned on that router
quiz.why: RAM is forgotten at reload. `copy running-config startup-config` is the command that makes a change persist.

quiz.q: Which pair is a host command followed by an IOS command that both help with 'who is this IPv4 neighbour?'
quiz.why: Those two display the ARP cache. nslookup is DNS; show version is software and uptime.

quiz.q: A ping to the default gateway fails, and the interface on the PC shows an APIPA address (169.254.x.x). A likely cause is:
options: The host did not get a DHCP lease, so it has no valid gateway either
IPv6 SLAAC has taken over IPv4
The MAC broadcast address has changed
SSH is misconfigured on a different floor
quiz.why: 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local/APIPA, used when DHCP has not provided an address. There will be no useful default gateway in that situation.

quiz.q: show version is the command you use when you want to know:
options: The software image and how long the device has been up
The list of DNS AAAA records
quiz.why: `show version` is identity and uptime (and memory, among other things). It is not the forwarding or ARP table.

quiz.q: A calm troubleshooting rule that prevents a lot of damage is:
options: Change one thing, then test, rather than changing five things at once
Always disable IPv4 before testing IPv6
Never look at interface lights, because they are misleading in every case
quiz.why: If you change several things, you cannot tell which change helped or which one made it worse. One change, one test.
